what_it_does: Most computers store numbers in binary — a compact code of zeros and ones where each digit's position carries a different weight (so '1011' means 11). Unary representation is a completely different encoding where a number N is simply N ones in a row (so 3 is '111'). Unary is surprisingly useful for certain low-power, noise-tolerant computing circuits because operations like addition become trivially simple. The catch is that converting a binary number into its unary form traditionally requires a comparator — a circuit that checks whether each possible value is less than or equal to the input — and those comparators are expensive in silicon area and power, especially when dealing with many inputs or higher precision. This paper proposes new circuits that produce the unary output without any comparators at all, instead using simpler alternative logic, and offers both an exact version and a faster approximate version.
